blocks.instructionalPurpose: Commit to a prediction, run the experiment, then explain what happened. Learner action: Use the model, complete its task, and explain what the representation shows.

accessibility.textAlternative: What happens to ice as it warms from -5 degrees C to 20 degrees C? Options: It melts; the particles remain water particles.; The particles themselves grow into liquid particles.. After you predict, the observation is shown. Compare your prediction with the observation and explain the role of energy.

blocks.instructionalPurpose: Heat or cool water and watch the particle arrangement and motion change. Learner action: Use the model, complete its task, and explain what the representation shows.

accessibility.textAlternative: Change temperature and compare solid, liquid and gas representations. This is a simplified model, not measured data. Below 0 °C water is a solid: particles packed in a pattern, vibrating in place. From 0 °C to 100 °C it is a liquid: particles close together, sliding past one another. At 100 °C and above it is a gas: particles far apart, moving quickly in all directions.

blocks.instructionalPurpose: Read measurements as a table and a line graph. Learner action: Describe the interval from minute 1 to minute 3 using only the plotted evidence. Explain why a temperature plateau does not mean energy transfer has stopped.

accessibility.textAlternative: Illustrative ice heating. Time 0 min: Temperature -5 C; Time 1 min: Temperature 0 C; Time 2 min: Temperature 0 C; Time 3 min: Temperature 0 C; Time 4 min: Temperature 10 C. A plateau can indicate a phase change; these data alone do not establish how much energy was supplied.
